title: Half the S&P's Earnings Gains This Year Are Just Cloud Giants' AI Spending
dek: Goldman Sachs calculates that roughly half of the S&P 500's earnings growth this year comes directly from cloud giants' AI capital spending; the market is betting not on today's sales, but on whether this money converts to revenue in three years.
why: Want to understand why U.S. stocks have shrugged off rate hikes, Iran conflict, and weak consumer spending yet remain fragile? This episode provides specific numbers and mechanisms instead of generic "AI bubble" talk.
who: Investors and buy-side analysts watching U.S. equity valuations and AI capex sustainability, plus anyone trying to understand why consumer stocks keep getting sold.
skip: 32:36–34:38: discussion of Manchester City financial violations and football league tangent unrelated to market mechanics; can skip.

points.h: Breadth collapse mirrors the internet bust, but does not reliably predict tops
points.body: The S&P 500 is only 0.5% from all-time highs, yet just 51.2% of its constituents trade above their 200-day moving average—the last time the market was this close to records with so few stocks participating was the day after the internet bubble burst. But Luke counters with precedent: in 1998, breadth was equally dire, yet the S&P went on to gain for two more years. Breadth alone does not determine tops.

points.h: Consumer stocks are now the proxy for betting against AI exuberance
points.body: Nike crashed from $180 in 2021 to $35; McDonald's, Walmart, and Costco face similar valuation compression. Luke's theory: these stocks became proxies for shorting software companies expected to be disrupted by AI. Walmart's steady monthly throughput resembles subscription ARR; Costco's membership fee is essentially recurring revenue. When AI stocks surge, the market needs something to punish.

points.h: Half of S&P earnings growth this year is cloud capex itself, not its monetization
points.body: Goldman Sachs estimates that roughly half of the S&P's earnings growth this year comes directly from cloud giants' AI capex spending. Valuations now hinge not on next year's sales expectations but on three-year-ahead sales. Economist Hanno Lustig goes further: to fully justify this spending, a handful of companies must eventually capture 9% of GDP in revenue—both Luke and Joe call this absurd. Nvidia has begun separately listing sovereign AI and robotics revenue streams in its earnings to argue the addressable market is broader than cloud capex alone.

points.h: Rising bond yields reflect surging growth, not uncontrolled inflation
points.body: Luke attributes the 10-year Treasury yield breaking 5% primarily to strong global growth pushing real rates higher, not inflation expectations spiraling. Breakeven inflation rates remain stable. This surprises him: the Fed has failed to keep inflation near its target for years, so you'd expect markets to discount central-bank credibility. Yet breakeven rates show no such skepticism.

points.h: Markets have moved too fast for shorts to build effective hedges
points.body: Luke sums up last year as TINA (There Is No Alternative); this year, it's prices and earnings rising too fast to hedge effectively. AI is compressing the timeline of economic events; add AI agents trading while humans sleep, and the market operates at an unprecedented pace. Robinhood retail net-buy data show peaks in June (around Micron earnings) and October last year (around Palantir, bitcoin, quantum compute hype), with September recovering to 89% of June's peak.

points.h: Negative free cash flow at giants demands increasingly creative financing tactics
points.body: Luke argues that once cloud giants' free cash flow turns negative, two paths remain: slow AI buildout, or get creative with financing. The latter is happening. He links this to Minsky moments: as long as the debt looks safe (cloud balance sheets, federal deficits), valuations hold. But that's exactly how "safe" tips into "unsafe."

points.h: This AI expansion is built on debt, not on AI-generated cash
points.body: Luke borrows from Wall Street Journal's Greg Ip: past internet giants funded expansion with their own cash machines—Facebook's ads, Google's search. This time is different. Oracle has no pure cash cow; it must borrow. Credit default swaps keep rising. Nvidia even steps in to boost credit for peers, trying to make all AI borrowers look equally safe.

points.h: AI has replaced real estate as the driver of economic cycles
points.body: Luke notes that wealth gains from equities now exceed those from real estate, a watershed moment. Real estate defined the business cycle because HELOCs and wealth effects flowed into consumption; the same logic now applies to AI—capex surges and wealth-effect surges emanate from here. He calls this abnormal: ultimately, downstream consumers must buy or the cycle breaks.
